rows: Employers must protect workers from health and safety risks.
PPE should be provided free of charge when risk assessment shows it is needed.
PPE is used for residual risk after higher-order controls have been applied.
Selection should match the hazard, task and wearer.
Different items of PPE should be compatible when worn together.
Workers need information, instruction and training in correct use.
PPE should be maintained, stored and replaced so it remains effective.
Employers should check that PPE is actually used as intended.
A CE or UKCA mark and issue record do not prove that PPE is suitable for a particular exposure.
Protection conclusions require hazard, required performance, fit, compatibility, condition, training and use evidence.
Dutyholders should identify and assess foreseeable legionella risks in water systems.
A competent person should help manage identified legionella risks.
Water systems should be designed, maintained and operated to prevent or control bacterial growth.
Risk assessment should consider water temperature, stagnation and sources of nutrients.
Control schemes should define responsibilities and operational precautions.
Monitoring and records should demonstrate that controls are being implemented.
Cleaning, treatment and maintenance may be required for relevant systems.
Risk assessment and control schemes should be reviewed when systems or conditions change.
A single temperature reading or recent service does not prove that a water system is adequately controlled.
System conclusions require design, use, temperatures, outlets, stagnation, treatment, monitoring and corrective-action evidence.
Cooling towers and evaporative condensers can generate aerosols capable of spreading legionella.
Appropriate measures are needed to prevent or control legionella risk.
Relevant cooling systems should be notified to the local authority as required.
Water treatment should control microbial growth, scale and corrosion.
Systems require planned cleaning, disinfection and maintenance.
Operating conditions and water quality should be monitored.
Drift control and physical condition affect the release of aerosols.
Loss of control should trigger prompt investigation and corrective action.
A local-authority notification or biocide result does not prove current control of a cooling system.
Conclusions require system design, water treatment, dosing, monitoring, drift, maintenance and incident evidence.
Work-related violence includes abuse, threats and assaults connected with work.
Employers should assess who may be harmed and how violence can arise.
Incident and near-miss records can help identify patterns of risk.
Work design, staffing, environment and contact arrangements can reduce risk.
Workers should receive information and training relevant to foreseeable violence.
Reporting and support arrangements should be clear and accessible.
Controls should consider lone workers and people dealing with the public.
Incidents should be reviewed so that risk controls can be improved.
A security guard or zero reported incidents does not prove that violence risk is adequately controlled.
Conclusions require task, clients, timing, location, staffing, history, controls, reporting and worker-feedback evidence.
